analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans offshore oil and gas drilling along the Atlantic coast and eastern Gulf of Mexico.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 63 cosponsors but never received a committee markup or a House floor vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The COAST Anti-Drilling Act would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to permanently bar the Interior Department from leasing any waters in the Mid-Atlantic, South Atlantic, North Atlantic, Straits of Florida, or Eastern Gulf of Mexico planning areas for oil, gas, or mineral drilling. That would lock in the status quo for beaches, fisheries, and tourism businesses along the Atlantic and eastern Gulf coasts, and take future drilling off the table by law rather than leaving it to each administration's five-year leasing plan. The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, sent to its energy subcommittee a month later, and sat there until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, beach tourism businesses, and commercial and recreational fishing industries along the Atlantic and eastern Gulf coasts would gain permanent legal protection from new offshore drilling and the spill risk it brings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal communities, fisheries, and tourism businesses

how_it_helps.text: The bill permanently prohibits the Interior Department from issuing any lease or authorization for exploration, development, or production of oil, natural gas, or other minerals in the Mid-Atlantic, South Atlantic, North Atlantic, Straits of Florida, and Eastern Gulf of Mexico planning areas.

Because the prohibition is written into the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act itself and applies 'notwithstanding any other provision of this section or any other law,' it cannot be undone by a future administration simply revising its five-year leasing plan.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would lose access to potential lease areas along the Atlantic coast and the eastern Gulf, and the federal Treasury would forgo any royalties those leases might have produced.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes the Interior Department's authority to lease these waters under any circumstances, so future energy development would be barred by statute regardless of new information about resources, technology, or need.

Domestic oil and gas production and federal royalty revenue from the affected planning areas would be foregone permanently, a real cost to an honest supporter of coastal protection to acknowledge, though no leases in these areas were being issued at the time.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is durable and direct for the coastal economies that depend on clean water and beaches, while the cost falls on a single industry and on hypothetical revenue that was not being collected anyway under the administration's existing plan. The main design criticism is that a permanent statutory ban is inflexible if circumstances change, but the bill's supporters saw that inflexibility as the point.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and its energy subcommittee without ever receiving a markup or a vote until the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone of New Jersey introduced the bill on January 8, 2019, the first day of the new Congress.
The House referred it to the Committee on Natural Resources the same day, and on February 5, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources.
No further action was taken on the bill before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill had 63 cosponsors, including 61 of 231 House Democrats and 2 of 197 House Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas producers are better off, since no statutory barrier was enacted and future administrations retain the legal authority to open these waters to leasing. Coastal communities remain protected only in practice, not in law, so their protection depends on which administration holds office.

for.name: Frank Pallone
for.role: House sponsor (D-NJ), chair of the Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 8, 2019 and recruited the initial cosponsors.

against.name: Raúl Grijalva
against.what_they_did: The committee received the bill the day it was introduced and referred it to a subcommittee, and no markup or floor consideration was ever scheduled for it during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the only record of support is the cosponsor list: 61 of 231 House Democrats signed on versus 2 of 197 House Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would permanently bar the industry from leasing five Atlantic and eastern Gulf planning areas, ending any prospect of drilling off the Atlantic coast. Its interest in keeping those waters open runs against the coastal communities that bear the spill risk.

Beach economies, charter fishing, and commercial fisheries along the Atlantic and eastern Gulf coasts would gain a permanent statutory shield against new drilling and the spill risk that comes with it. The bill's own title names tourism as a beneficiary.
